habitat: Dense, mature old-growth forests, especially hilly rainforest and other large, relatively unfragmented forest areas.
distribution: Forests of the Indian subcontinent, Bhutan, Nepal, mainland Southeast Asia and Sumatra, with fragmented populations in parts of the Western Ghats and Himalayan foothills.
diet: Predominantly fruit, especially figs, but also small mammals, birds, reptiles and insects.
behavior: Usually occurs in pairs or small parties, with larger groups sometimes gathering at fruiting trees. It is an important seed disperser and can travel considerable distances between feeding and roosting sites.
breeding: Forms monogamous pairs. The female seals herself inside a large tree cavity and depends on the male for food while incubating the eggs and raising the young. A clutch usually contains one or two eggs.
conservation: IUCN Red List: Vulnerable. Major threats include habitat loss from deforestation and hunting for meat and body parts.
interestingFacts: It is one of the largest hornbill species.
Its casque and large bill give it a distinctive silhouette.
Great hornbills can live for decades in captivity, with records approaching 50 years.

habitat: Subtropical and tropical moist lowland forests, including dry and semi-evergreen forests, deciduous forests, secondary forests, plantations, and woodlands. It can tolerate some disturbed habitats.
distribution: Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, from India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Tibet through Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore to Indonesia, Brunei and islands of the Sunda region.
diet: Mainly fruit, including figs, berries, rambutans, palm fruits and other fleshy fruits. It also eats large insects, small reptiles, amphibians, fish, bats, small birds, eggs and nestlings.
behavior: A mostly canopy-dwelling hornbill that often forages in pairs or small groups. Outside the breeding season it may feed in flocks and is an important disperser of large seeds. Its calls include harsh crackles, screeches and crow-like or braying sounds.
breeding: Usually monogamous and typically begins breeding around February, with breeding generally occurring from January to June depending on location. The female seals herself inside a tree cavity, leaving a narrow opening through which the male delivers food. The chicks remain in the nest for several months.
conservation: IUCN Red List: Least Concern. The species has a very wide range and is relatively adaptable, but logging reduces suitable nesting and fruiting trees. Hunting and capture for pets also affect some populations. Captive breeding, artificial nest sites and reintroduction are used in some areas.
interestingFacts: It has the largest geographic range of the five species in the genus Anthracoceros.
It is an important seed disperser because its large gape allows it to carry and disperse relatively large seeds.
Females seal themselves into nest cavities during breeding, relying on the male to bring food through a small opening.
The species has recolonized Singapore after becoming locally extinct there in the 1960s.

thaiName: นกกระจอกบ้าน
habitat: Human-dominated environments such as towns, cities, villages, farmland and gardens. It is absent mainly from dense forest and tundra and can also occur away from people in open country.
distribution: Native across much of Europe, the Mediterranean region, northern Africa and large parts of Asia, with extensive introductions making it widespread in many other parts of the world.
diet: Mostly seeds of cereals and weeds, supplemented by fruits, buds and other plant material. Adults also eat insects and other small invertebrates, while nestlings are fed mainly insects.
behavior: Highly adaptable and commonly social, often foraging and roosting around human settlements. It can exploit a wide range of food sources and frequently scavenges human food waste.
breeding: Usually nests in cavities or sheltered spaces around buildings and other structures. Pairs can produce multiple broods in a breeding season, and young are fed a high proportion of insects.
conservation: IUCN Red List: Least Concern globally, although substantial declines have occurred in some regions, particularly in parts of Europe and other urbanized areas.
interestingFacts: House sparrows are closely associated with humans but are not completely dependent on human habitation.
They can survive in very dry environments and have adaptations that help them cope with limited water.
They can use buildings, warehouses and other artificial structures as nesting or shelter sites.
